command: Run scripts/setup-agent-edit-probe.py, start an isolated OpenCode server in the fixture directory on port 18089, then node scripts/probe-agent-edit.mjs
conclusion: The successful probe changed subtraction to addition and passed independent Python assertions. Instrumentation showed the failed configuration sent no tools. Its PowerShell-generated permission rules placed the wildcard deny after the allow rules; OpenCode applies the last matching rule, so it overrode them. An explicit tool_call capability was also added before the successful run; the individual contribution of each change was not isolated. Harness permissions are not an OS sandbox, and one trivial fixture does not establish coding quality or security. A second run using the checked-in setup script also passed the assertions.
next: Repeat on a diverse coding benchmark, verify permission-denial behavior and memory use; keep the demo harness read-only until a safe writable workspace is designed.

The monitor does not reserve memory or enforce a limit.
next: Collect baseline-versus-load time series and connect reliable monitoring to a fail-closed admission controller before additional model loads.

conclusion: After switching away from memory mapping, the Gemma process working set was about 1.0 GiB versus about 9.5 GiB in a prior snapshot, and available physical memory rose substantially. Adapter shared GPU accounting increased by about 0.77 GiB compared with EXP-020, exceeding the experimental 256 MiB growth threshold. This is not a controlled A/B peak study, and shared allocations do not prove model-weight eviction. Both streaming and non-streaming read-tool probes succeeded. The current mode does not satisfy the conservative shared-memory guard and must not be claimed as validated under the full budget.
next: Measure controlled cold and warm peaks, identify the shared allocation, compare quality and latency, and implement enforced admission rather than relying on snapshots.
